messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The event happened at 04:17, in the humid dark before dawn. Thomas, then a twenty-three-year-old helicopter door gunner in the Solomon Islands campaign, was riding the starboard edge of a low-altitude insertion when the rotor wash caught a palm frond and slapped it against his face. The frond was wet and fibrous, a particular texture—rough and yielding at once—and before he could brush it away, the world turned to noise. The aircraft took fire from the tree line. The man beside him, a loader named Kele, took a round through the throat and collapsed against Thomas’s shoulder, his blood warm and slick on Thomas’s cheek and hands. The helicopter yawed hard, the pilot screaming into the intercom, and Thomas spent the next forty-seven seconds firing into the green-black dark until the bird cleared the LZ. He does not remember landing. He remembers the texture of the frond, the wet weight of Kele’s body, and the exact pitch of the rotors as they strained through the evasion.

Forty years later, Thomas is an airline pilot. He still flies. He has to. The pension isn’t enough, and his wife, Lani, has made it clear she will not watch him retire into the armchair she already calls his “bunker.” But flying has become a kind of endurance. Every time he steps into the cockpit, the sound of the engines—a low turbine whine that vibrates through the floor—can, without warning, collapse the distance between present and past. He will be running through the pre-flight checklist and suddenly he is back in the Huey, the rotor blades chopping the air, and the terror hits him in the chest like a physical blow. The memory feels alien, as though it belongs to someone else, a younger man who did things Thomas cannot reconcile with the man he is now, but the terror is his own, and it is immediate. He has learned to grip the yoke harder, to breathe through it, but he cannot control when it comes. A texture—the rough fabric of his uniform cuff against his wrist—can do it. The time of day can do it. The hour before dawn, when the sky is that particular bruised purple, is the worst. He has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, and that this is not paranoia but simple truth, because the world proved it to him once and has been proving it ever since.

He now scans for exits as soon as he enters any room. He does it automatically, without thought, but the scanning itself keeps the memory near. The more he scans, the more he sees threat, and the more he sees threat, the more the memory rushes back—the helicopter banking, the sudden movements of the crew, the way Kele’s head snapped back. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. A flight attendant reaching quickly for an overhead bin can make his heart spike. He has come to believe there is something wrong with him as a person, that he used to be happy but is now always miserable, and this belief makes the world feel even more dangerous, which makes him scan harder, which pulls the memory closer again. The loop tightens. The more the memory intrudes, the more he appraises himself as broken, and the more he appraises himself as broken, the more he notices triggers everywhere—the texture of his leather seat, the sound of a helicopter on the news, the 4:17 glow of his bedside clock. He avoids the news. He avoids the texture of certain fabrics. He avoids leaving the house after dark, because he finds it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and the night vigilance makes him irritable with Lani, which makes him feel more defective, which makes the memory more likely to surface.

What finally brought him to help was a single moment in the cockpit last month. The time of day was 04:17. He was taxiing toward the runway, and the first officer made a sudden movement to adjust the radio. Thomas felt the memory arrive without warning—full sensory, full terror—and for a moment he could not remember which aircraft he was in. He landed the plane safely, but he sat in the parking bay for twenty minutes afterward, shaking. He is afraid he will lose his medical clearance. He is afraid Lani will leave. But what frightens him most is the thought that the memory will keep coming, and that one day he will not be able to land the plane.
